topics.title: Eye and ear tests
topics.recognize: Eyes: acuity/fields, tonometry and retinal examination identify different problems. Ears: otoscopy, audiometry and Weber/Rinne distinguish obstruction, conduction and nerve loss.
topics.act: Explain the test, compare both sides and report sudden vision or hearing changes promptly.
topics.remember: Match the test to function: pressure is not acuity; air/bone conduction helps classify hearing loss.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a chart, pressure gauge and tuning fork test different eye and ear functions.

handout.caption: From your guides · Vision patterns & hearing clues

topics.title: Impaired vision
topics.recognize: Reduced functional vision can persist despite correction; assess what the patient can actually see and do.
topics.act: Orient to the room, announce your presence, maintain consistent placement and offer assistance with mobility and self-care.
topics.remember: Speak directly to the patient. Support independence rather than assuming blindness means total loss of vision.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a fixed path through a dim room represents orientation and consistent placement.

handout.caption: From your guides · Vision loss patterns

topics.title: Glaucoma
topics.recognize: Open-angle disease gradually damages peripheral vision. Acute angle closure causes severe eye pain, halos, blurred vision and nausea.
topics.act: Treat sudden painful visual changes as an emergency; reinforce prescribed pressure-lowering drops and follow-up.
topics.remember: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve; established loss is irreversible. Chronic disease can be silent before substantial loss occurs.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a pressure gauge squeezes an optic cable: glaucoma threatens peripheral vision.

topics.title: Cataracts
topics.recognize: A cloudy lens causes painless progressive blur, glare and difficulty seeing at night.
topics.act: After surgery, use ordered drops and protection; avoid pressure or straining and report severe pain or worsening vision.
topics.remember: Cataracts affect the lens, unlike glaucoma's optic-nerve injury. Surgical replacement improves vision; postoperative pain should not simply be dismissed.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a cloudy window is the opaque lens; replacing the pane restores clarity.

handout.caption: From your guides · Eye disorders: what changes

topics.title: Retinal detachment
topics.recognize: Sudden flashes, new floaters or a curtain over vision suggest the retina is separating.
topics.act: Arrange urgent ophthalmic evaluation; follow procedure-specific positioning and restrictions after repair.
topics.remember: Usually painless does not mean harmless. With an intraocular gas bubble, air travel and nitrous oxide can dangerously expand the bubble until cleared.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a falling curtain crosses a flashing window: sudden retinal symptoms need urgent evaluation.

topics.title: Macular degeneration
topics.recognize: Central vision becomes distorted or blurred while peripheral vision may remain; a straight-line grid can appear wavy.
topics.act: Report new distortion promptly, support low-vision aids and reinforce specialist monitoring and prescribed treatment.
topics.remember: Dry disease is degenerative; wet disease involves abnormal leaking vessels and can deteriorate rapidly. Central loss interferes with reading and recognizing faces.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a dark spot hides the center of a clock while its outer rim stays visible.

topics.title: Diabetic retinopathy
topics.recognize: Retinal microvascular injury may be asymptomatic initially, later causing blur, floaters or visual loss.
topics.act: Reinforce dilated retinal screening and glucose, blood-pressure and lipid management; urgently report sudden changes.
topics.remember: Absence of symptoms does not exclude damage. Laser, injections or surgery depend on retinal findings; diabetes care and eye surveillance work together.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine leaking tiny retinal pipes represent diabetic vessel damage and screening before symptoms.

handout.caption: From your guides · Changes Inside the Retina

topics.title: Conjunctivitis
topics.recognize: Redness and discharge suggest conjunctival inflammation; itching favors allergy, while infectious patterns vary.
topics.act: Use hand hygiene, separate towels, avoid sharing eye products and follow prescribed therapy; remove contact lenses until cleared.
topics.remember: Significant pain, photophobia or reduced vision needs evaluation beyond routine conjunctivitis. Antibiotics do not treat viral or allergic causes.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a red window with separate towels represents irritated eyes and infection control.

topics.title: Hearing loss
topics.recognize: Conductive loss disrupts sound transmission; sensorineural loss involves the cochlea or nerve. Assess onset, laterality and communication needs.
topics.act: Face the patient, reduce background noise, speak clearly and verify hearing-aid function; report sudden loss urgently.
topics.remember: Shouting can distort speech. Use written or visual supports and teach-back rather than treating a missed question as confusion.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a blocked hallway versus a damaged cable separates conductive and sensorineural hearing loss.

handout.caption: From your guides · Ear anatomy & hearing loss

topics.title: Cerumen impaction
topics.recognize: Wax can cause conductive hearing loss, fullness or discomfort; inspect the canal and tympanic membrane.
topics.act: Use appropriate removal methods; avoid irrigation with suspected perforation, tubes, relevant ear surgery or significant infection unless cleared.
topics.remember: Do not push cotton swabs into the canal. Distinguish wax blockage from sudden sensorineural hearing loss requiring urgent assessment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a wax plug blocks a sound tunnel; pushing it deeper worsens the obstruction.

topics.title: Otitis externa
topics.recognize: External-canal inflammation causes pain, often increased by pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus; moisture and trauma contribute.
topics.act: Keep the ear dry, administer prescribed topical therapy correctly and avoid inserting objects.
topics.remember: Diabetes or immunosuppression plus severe persistent pain warrants prompt evaluation for invasive infection. This is a canal problem, not middle-ear fluid.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a wet outer tunnel hurts when its door is tugged: external-canal inflammation.

handout.caption: From your guides · What an Ear Exam Shows

topics.title: Tympanic membrane perforation
topics.recognize: Trauma, pressure changes or infection can perforate the eardrum, causing sudden pain, drainage and reduced hearing.
topics.act: Keep the ear dry and avoid unapproved drops, irrigation and forceful pressure changes; arrange evaluation.
topics.remember: Some perforations heal spontaneously; persistent defects may need repair. Sudden severe vertigo or major hearing loss needs urgent assessment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a torn drum needs a dry protective cover, not water forced through it.

topics.title: Otitis media and middle-ear surgery
topics.recognize: Acute middle-ear infection causes pain and an abnormal tympanic membrane; chronic disease can produce persistent drainage and hearing loss.
topics.act: Give prescribed treatment and protect the repaired ear after surgery; monitor facial movement, hearing, drainage and worsening vertigo.
topics.remember: Follow procedure-specific positioning, water and pressure restrictions. Persistent drainage or cholesteatoma can damage middle-ear structures and may require surgery.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine fluid behind an eardrum and a repaired bridge cue middle-ear infection and postoperative protection.

handout.caption: From your guides · Otitis media

topics.title: Ménière disease
topics.recognize: Episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness reflect excess inner-ear fluid.
topics.act: During attacks, prevent falls and reduce movement/stimulation; administer prescribed symptom treatment and reinforce the individualized diet/medication plan.
topics.remember: Vertigo is episodic and hearing can progressively decline. Teach safe mobility and avoidance of hazardous activity while symptomatic.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a sloshing inner-ear bowl rings and spins: fullness, tinnitus and episodic vertigo.

topics.title: Vertigo, tinnitus, BPPV and ototoxicity
topics.recognize: Vertigo is a false movement sensation; tinnitus is perceived sound. Brief position-triggered vertigo suggests BPPV, while ototoxic drugs can impair hearing or balance.
topics.act: Prevent falls, review medications and report new hearing changes; use prescribed repositioning maneuvers for BPPV.
topics.remember: BPPV involves displaced inner-ear crystals. Persistent neurologic findings or severe new symptoms require evaluation beyond a benign ear diagnosis.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine loose crystals tumble with head movement; a warning label flags ototoxic medication.

handout.caption: From your guides · Hearing & Inner-Ear Disorders

topics.title: Immune assessment and CBC
covers: Variables that affect the immune system
topics.recognize: Age, nutrition, chronic illness, medications and exposures affect immune defense. Leukopenia is low WBC; leukocytosis is high WBC; neutropenia specifically reduces neutrophils.
topics.act: Interpret the differential/ANC and clinical trend, assess infection sites and urgently report fever with impaired defenses.
topics.remember: A high WBC alone does not establish bacterial infection; a low neutrophil count can blunt expected inflammatory findings.
topics.sn: Labs - Lab Values - WBC & Coagulation Panel
topics.mnemonic: Imagine count each kind of guard: total WBC and neutrophil numbers answer different questions.

topics.title: Isolation, neutropenia and device infections
topics.recognize: Neutropenia increases infection risk; central lines, urinary catheters and ventilation create device-associated infection routes.
topics.act: Use appropriate transmission precautions, meticulous hand hygiene and device care. Review necessity daily: sterile line care, closed urinary drainage and ventilator oral care/head elevation.
topics.remember: CLABSI: protect insertion/hub sites. CAUTI: keep flow unobstructed and bag below bladder. VAP: oral hygiene, mobility and liberation protocols. Routine chlorhexidine oral care is not recommended here.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine guards inspect a line, catheter and breathing tube to block three device-infection routes.

handout.caption: From your guides · Infection Precautions: Match The Route

topics.title: HIV diagnosis and AIDS
topics.recognize: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; opportunistic infections and certain malignancies signal advanced disease. AIDS can be defined by CD4 criteria or an AIDS-defining condition.
topics.act: Support testing, antiretroviral adherence and prompt infection evaluation.
topics.remember: ELISA/Western blot appears in course terminology, but current testing uses antigen/antibody screening, differentiation testing and nucleic-acid testing when indicated; use the actual laboratory algorithm.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a shrinking CD4 guard team represents immune loss; tests identify infection and stage.

handout.caption: From your guides · ELISA & HIV Screening

topics.title: HIV transmission, stages and monitoring
topics.recognize: HIV transmits through specific body fluids, not casual contact. Acute infection may resemble a viral illness; chronic infection may remain silent before advanced immunodeficiency.
topics.act: Teach prevention, sustained ART and urgent evaluation after exposure; PEP is time-sensitive and must start within 72 hours when indicated.
topics.remember: Viral load measures replication/treatment response; CD4 count measures immune status. Undetectable sexual transmission risk depends on sustained viral suppression.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a viral counter measures replication while a separate guard counter measures CD4 defense.

handout.caption: From your guides · HIV: viral load vs CD4 count

topics.title: Infectious-disease priorities
topics.recognize: Look for exposure, susceptible host, local infection and systemic deterioration; immunocompromised clients may show subtle signs.
topics.act: Assess ABCs/perfusion, apply appropriate precautions and obtain ordered cultures without delaying urgent treatment.
topics.remember: Identify the organism and transmission route instead of assuming every fever needs the same isolation or antibiotic. Reassess response, hydration and organ function.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a breached gate prompts exposure history, infection precautions and a perfusion check.

handout.caption: From your guides · Sepsis: Urgent Care Priorities

topics.title: Chain of infection
topics.recognize: The chain requires an infectious agent, reservoir, exit route, transmission method, entry route and susceptible host.
topics.act: Break links with hand hygiene, PPE, cleaning, safe sharps, respiratory hygiene, vaccination and appropriate device care.
topics.remember: Choose an intervention that interrupts the relevant link. Standard precautions apply to everyone; contact, droplet or airborne measures depend on suspected transmission.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine break one link in a six-link chain to interrupt infection transmission.

handout.caption: From your guides · Break the chain of infection

topics.title: C. difficile
topics.recognize: Antibiotic exposure can permit toxin-producing C. difficile to cause watery diarrhea, abdominal pain and severe colitis.
topics.act: Use contact precautions, appropriate handwashing and sporicidal cleaning; monitor fluids and give prescribed targeted therapy.
topics.remember: Alcohol sanitizer does not reliably kill spores. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and report distention, hypotension or worsening illness promptly.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine spores cling to a door despite sanitizer; soap and sporicidal cleaning target them.

handout.caption: From your guides · Transmission-based precautions

topics.title: MRSA and VRE
topics.recognize: MRSA resists common beta-lactams; VRE resists vancomycin. Colonization and active infection are different findings.
topics.act: Follow culture-directed therapy and facility contact precautions, protect wounds and devices, and perform hand/environmental hygiene.
topics.remember: An organism's resistance pattern determines effective therapy; colonization alone does not automatically mean antibiotics are needed. Communicate precautions during transfers.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine resistant shields deflect the wrong antibiotic; culture results select the effective tool.

handout.caption: From your guides · The Bacterial Defense Team

topics.title: Immunizations, diarrhea and emerging infections
topics.recognize: Vaccination history, travel, food/water and outbreak exposures guide risk assessment. Diarrhea can rapidly compromise fluids and electrolytes.
topics.act: Use current vaccine guidance, restore hydration, monitor severity and apply exposure-specific testing/precautions; report suspected outbreaks through the required channels.
topics.remember: Immune status affects vaccine selection. New or emerging infections require updated public-health guidance rather than assumptions based on older transmission rules.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a vaccine shield, water jug and travel map cue immunity, hydration and exposure assessment.

handout.caption: From your guides · Immunizations

topics.title: Four hypersensitivity mechanisms
topics.recognize: Type I is immediate IgE-mediated allergy; type II targets cells; type III involves immune complexes; type IV is delayed T-cell activity.
topics.act: Identify the trigger and severity; rapidly treat airway or circulatory compromise rather than waiting to classify the mechanism.
topics.remember: ACID: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed. Timing and organ involvement distinguish mechanisms; not every rash is anaphylaxis.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine four immune workbenches hold an alarm, damaged cell, complexes and a delayed clock: ACID.

handout.caption: From your guides · Hypersensitivity I–IV: see the mechanism + ACID memory

topics.title: Anaphylaxis
topics.recognize: Sudden airway swelling, wheeze, hypotension or multisystem symptoms after exposure indicate a potentially fatal reaction.
topics.act: Give IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol, activate help, support airway/oxygenation and circulation, and monitor for recurrence.
topics.remember: Antihistamines are adjuncts, not substitutes for epinephrine. A skin rash may be absent; teach trigger avoidance and correct auto-injector use.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an airway gate slams shut; the epinephrine emergency bell calls for immediate action.

handout.caption: From your guides · Anaphylaxis: why epinephrine comes first

topics.title: Urticaria and food allergy
topics.recognize: Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals; food allergy may progress to breathing difficulty, swelling, vomiting or circulatory compromise.
topics.act: Assess airway and systemic involvement first; use prescribed symptom therapy for isolated hives and emergency epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
topics.remember: Teach label reading, avoiding known allergens and carrying the emergency plan. Do not equate every food intolerance with immune-mediated allergy.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine itchy clouds become an airway alarm when allergy involves breathing or circulation.

handout.caption: From your guides · Immune and inflammatory signs

topics.title: Latex allergy
topics.recognize: Latex exposure may cause local dermatitis or immediate systemic allergy; repeated healthcare exposure increases risk.
topics.act: Identify and remove latex sources, use latex-free supplies and document the allergy; urgently treat airway or circulatory symptoms.
topics.remember: Delayed contact dermatitis differs from immediate IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. Some food cross-reactions can occur, but assess actual history rather than assuming all related foods are unsafe.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a crossed-out latex glove protects the patient from the known trigger.

topics.title: Rheumatic disease
topics.recognize: Inflammation or autoimmune activity can affect joints and other organs; evaluate pain, stiffness, fatigue, function and systemic findings.
topics.act: Balance activity and rest, preserve mobility, monitor medication effects and screen for infection or organ involvement.
topics.remember: A rheumatic diagnosis is not just joint pain. Connect disease activity, treatment-related immune suppression and functional limitations to individualized care.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an inflamed joint sends warning lights to other organs: rheumatic disease can be systemic.

handout.caption: From your guides · Rheumatoid Arthritis

topics.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus
topics.recognize: Autoimmune inflammation may cause fatigue, joint pain, photosensitive rash and renal or other organ involvement.
topics.act: Monitor kidney findings and flare symptoms; reinforce sun protection, medication adherence and infection precautions appropriate to therapy.
topics.remember: Distinguish infection from a flare before attributing fever to lupus. Organ involvement determines urgency and treatment; avoid abrupt steroid withdrawal.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a butterfly rests under a sun shield while a kidney alarm watches organ involvement.

topics.title: Gout and fibromyalgia
topics.recognize: Gout causes acute inflammatory joint pain from urate crystals; fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, fatigue and sleep problems without inflammatory joint destruction.
topics.act: For gout, use prescribed anti-inflammatory therapy and long-term urate management when indicated. For fibromyalgia, support graded activity, sleep and multimodal symptom control.
topics.remember: Do not treat fibromyalgia as crystal arthritis; acute gout relief and prevention use different strategies.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine sharp crystals in one joint contrast with widespread aching and a broken sleep clock.

handout.caption: From your guides · Four pain patterns: RA, lupus, gout, fibromyalgia

topics.title: Burn mechanisms and deep injury
topics.recognize: Thermal injury damages tissue; electrical injury can hide deep muscle damage, dysrhythmia and myoglobin-related kidney injury. Chemicals continue damaging tissue while present.
topics.act: Ensure scene safety, remove the exposure appropriately and monitor ECG, urine and limb perfusion. Deep compartment pressure may require fasciotomy.
topics.remember: Visible skin injury can underestimate electrical damage. Fasciotomy releases fascia; escharotomy releases constricting burn eschar.
topics.sn: Burns - Types & Care for minor burns
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a small surface spark hides deep damage; chemical droplets keep burning until removed.

topics.title: Emergent burn resuscitation
covers: Parkland formula (standard 4mL x kg x TBSA%)
topics.recognize: Capillary leak shifts fluid into tissues, causing edema and intravascular depletion; severe burns also affect perfusion and GI function.
topics.act: Prioritize airway, ordered fluids and hourly perfusion/urine reassessment; consider escharotomy for constricting circumferential burns.
topics.remember: Course Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA over 24 hours, half within 8 hours of injury, not arrival. Actual resuscitation follows current orders and response rather than formula alone.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine leaking vessels empty the circulation; the fluid clock begins at injury time.

topics.title: Burn depth, appearance and severity
topics.recognize: Superficial burns are red and painful; partial-thickness burns may blister; full-thickness burns can appear leathery and have reduced sensation. Extent, depth, location and inhalation injury determine severity.
topics.act: Assess cleaned wound depth, perfusion and sensation, prevent hypothermia and consider critical location, age and inhalation injury when judging severity.
topics.remember: Do not count superficial erythema in resuscitation TBSA. Deep burns can be less painful.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine skin layers beside a body map separate burn depth from percentage of area.

topics.title: Inhalation injury
topics.recognize: Enclosed-space exposure, facial burns, soot, hoarseness or stridor raise airway concern; swelling may progress after the initial assessment.
topics.act: Give indicated high-concentration oxygen, obtain urgent airway evaluation and prepare for early airway protection when needed.
topics.remember: A reassuring conventional pulse-oximeter reading does not exclude carbon-monoxide poisoning. Airway injury and toxic inhalation can occur with little visible skin burn.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine smoke enters a swelling doorway: protect the airway before the opening narrows further.

topics.title: Burn phases and changing priorities
topics.recognize: Emergent: capillary leak and shock. Acute: fluid return, wound management and infection risk. Rehabilitation: function, scarring and adaptation.
topics.act: Reassess respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, GI, temperature and mobility effects as the phase changes.
topics.remember: A plan appropriate during fluid loss may need revision when fluid returns to circulation. Nursing priorities follow physiology rather than a fixed calendar alone.
topics.sn: Burns II - Major burns patho, signs & Treatments
topics.mnemonic: Imagine three stations show resuscitation, wound healing and rehabilitation as changing burn priorities.

topics.title: Acute burn care and rehabilitation
topics.recognize: After stabilization, open wounds, pain, infection, hypermetabolism, stiffness and psychosocial distress dominate.
topics.act: Premedicate for wound care; support high-protein/calorie nutrition, aseptic dressings, debridement and ordered topical therapy. Protect grafts initially, then advance prescribed range of motion, splinting and mobility.
topics.remember: Pressure garments/scar care follow healing and specialist orders. Teach wound changes, infection warning signs, home exercise and coping support; grafting covers wounds while debridement removes devitalized tissue.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a healing workshop combines dressings, protein, movement and support after burn stabilization.

topics.title: Burn wound care choices
topics.recognize: Wound depth, perfusion, contamination, drainage and healing determine the dressing and treatment plan.
topics.act: Clean and debride as ordered; give analgesia before procedures, use prescribed topical agents and protect viable tissue/grafts.
topics.remember: No single topical agent or dressing fits every burn. Document wound appearance and response, monitor systemic infection and teach safe home care with the burn team's instructions.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a dressing toolbox matches wound depth and healing rather than using one covering for every burn.

topics.title: TBSA: rule of nines and palmar estimate
topics.recognize: Adult rule of nines: head/neck and each arm 9%; each leg, anterior trunk and posterior trunk 18%; perineum 1%. The patient’s palm including fingers is approximately 1% TBSA.
topics.act: Use the adult body map for larger areas and palmar estimation for small scattered burns.
topics.remember: Count partial/full-thickness burns, not superficial redness, for resuscitation TBSA. Children need age-adjusted assessment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an adult body map stamped 9, 18 and 1; a palm stamp estimates small scattered areas.

topics.title: Addison disease and adrenal crisis
topics.recognize: Low cortisol causes weakness, hypotension and hypoglycemia; primary adrenal failure also loses aldosterone, causing sodium loss and potassium retention. Crisis can progress to shock.
topics.act: Urgently support circulation with prescribed fluids and IV glucocorticoids; monitor glucose, electrolytes, ECG and urine output.
topics.remember: Primary disease can cause hyperpigmentation. Teach lifelong replacement, the prescribed stress-dose plan and never abruptly stopping chronic steroids.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an empty hormone tank leaks salt and water; crisis needs fluids and prescribed steroids.

handout.caption: From your guides · Addison vs Cushing in pictures

topics.title: Cushing syndrome and disease
topics.recognize: Excess cortisol causes central weight gain, thin skin/bruising, muscle weakness, hyperglycemia and infection risk.
topics.act: Monitor glucose, blood pressure, skin and infection; protect fragile tissues and follow the steroid taper or endocrine treatment plan.
topics.remember: Cushing syndrome means excess cortisol from any cause; Cushing disease specifically means a pituitary ACTH source. Exogenous steroids are a common cause.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an overflowing cortisol tank adds central weight while thinning skin and weakening muscles.

handout.caption: From your guides · Adrenal cortex — Addison vs Cushing

topics.title: Pheochromocytoma
topics.recognize: A catecholamine-secreting tumor can cause episodic severe hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
topics.act: Monitor hemodynamics and follow specialist preparation for surgery; avoid provoking catecholamine release.
topics.remember: When ordered, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; isolated beta blockade can worsen hypertension. Plasma or urine metanephrine testing helps evaluate the suspected tumor.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an adrenal alarm sprays catecholamines: headache, sweating and pressure spikes.

topics.title: Hypothyroidism and myxedema coma
topics.recognize: Low thyroid activity causes fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation and slowed heart rate. Myxedema coma adds altered consciousness, hypothermia and hypoventilation.
topics.act: Support airway/ventilation and give prescribed thyroid replacement and emergency treatment; monitor cardiac response.
topics.remember: Primary disease generally has high TSH with low thyroid hormone; secondary disease reflects pituitary dysfunction. Severe hypothyroidism can be life-threatening even without literal coma.
topics.sn: Hyper & Hypothyroid - Patho, s s causes
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a slowed cold clock represents low thyroid activity; failing breathing is the emergency signal.

topics.title: Hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm
topics.recognize: Heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor and tachycardia suggest excess thyroid hormone; fever, severe tachycardia and altered mental status suggest storm.
topics.act: Escalate urgently, support ABCs and administer ordered antithyroid, rate-control, cooling and supportive treatment.
topics.remember: Thyroid storm is a clinical emergency. Follow medication sequencing; iodine is given after antithyroid medication when prescribed, not as a stand-alone first step.
topics.sn: Hyper & Hypothyroid - Patho, s s causes
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a hot racing clock represents thyroid excess; storm adds dangerous systemic acceleration.

topics.title: DI versus SIADH
topics.recognize: DI loses large amounts of dilute urine, risking dehydration and hypernatremia. SIADH retains water, causing dilutional hyponatremia with concentrated urine.
topics.act: Trend sodium, neurologic status, intake/output and daily weight; follow prescribed fluid and hormone treatment.
topics.remember: DI: water escapes. SIADH: water stays. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia needs urgent controlled correction; rapid sodium shifts can cause neurologic injury.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an open drain represents DI; a closed drain represents SIADH water retention.

topics.title: Type 1 and type2 diabetes
topics.recognize: Type 1 usually involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction and severe insulin deficiency. Type 2 combines insulin resistance with progressive loss of beta-cell function.
topics.act: Monitor glucose and symptoms, teach the individualized medication/meal/activity plan and confirm safe self-management.
topics.remember: Type 1 requires insulin replacement. Age and body size alone cannot distinguish the type; either type can develop acute hyperglycemic emergencies.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a missing insulin key differs from a resistant lock: type 1 deficiency versus type 2 resistance.

topics.title: Insulin timing and safety
topics.recognize: Insulin formulations differ in onset, peak and duration; strongest activity increases hypoglycemia risk.
topics.act: Verify product, concentration, dose and route. Coordinate meal-related insulin with food and check glucose when symptoms occur.
topics.remember: Rapid, regular, intermediate and basal products have different profiles. Mixing, storage and meal rules are product-specific; long-acting products do not share a universal peak or snack time.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine different insulin clocks peak at different times; food and glucose checks follow the actual product.

topics.title: Oral diabetes medications
topics.recognize: Metformin lowers liver glucose output; sulfonylureas/meglitinides increase insulin release; TZDs improve sensitivity; alpha-glucosidase inhibitors slow digestion; DPP-4 drugs enhance incretins; SGLT2 drugs increase urinary glucose.
topics.act: Watch for metformin GI/renal concerns, secretagogue hypoglycemia, TZD edema/heart failure, digestive effects, persistent abdominal pain and SGLT2 genital infection/ketoacidosis.
topics.remember: Match teaching to the exact drug and kidney/heart status, not a single rule for every diabetes tablet.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine six drug tools lower glucose differently; each carries its own adverse-effect tag.

topics.title: DKA versus HHS
topics.recognize: DKA combines ketones and acidosis; HHS causes marked hyperosmolar dehydration without significant ketosis. Both can alter consciousness; overlap and euglycemic DKA occur.
topics.act: Begin prescribed fluids, check potassium before insulin and repeatedly monitor glucose, electrolytes, perfusion and mental status.
topics.remember: Correct low potassium before starting insulin per prescribed protocol; total-body stores may be depleted even when serum potassium is high.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an acid kettle marks DKA; a concentrated dry tank marks HHS; both need fluid and electrolyte assessment.

topics.title: Diabetes sick-day plan
topics.recognize: Illness can raise glucose, while poor intake or some medicines cause lows; vomiting and dehydration increase risk.
topics.act: Check glucose more often, check ketones as directed, maintain fluids and follow medication/contact instructions. Type 1 patients still need basal insulin.
topics.remember: Breathing difficulty, confusion, persistent vomiting or inability to retain fluids needs urgent help. Use an individualized written plan, not a blanket rule to stop all medicines.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a sick-day checklist keeps basal insulin, fluids and frequent checks beside an emergency bell.

handout.caption: From your guides · Insulin — safe administration and home care

topics.title: Hypoglycemia
topics.recognize: Glucose below 70 mg/dL can cause sweating, shaking, hunger, palpitations, confusion or reduced consciousness.
topics.act: If awake and able to swallow, give 15 g rapid carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes; repeat if still low. If swallowing is unsafe, obtain emergency help and use prescribed glucagon or IV glucose.
topics.remember: Never give oral food/drink to an unconscious patient. Treat symptoms promptly rather than waiting for a predicted insulin peak.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a low-glucose alarm leads to sugar only through a safe swallowing gate.

handout.caption: From your guides · Insulin peaks & hypoglycemia risk

topics.title: Long-term diabetes complications
topics.recognize: Chronic vascular and nerve injury affects eyes, kidneys, heart, brain and feet; neuropathy can hide injury.
topics.act: Reinforce retinal and kidney screening, cardiovascular risk control and daily foot checks. Protect feet with fitted shoes and report wounds or color changes.
topics.remember: Avoid barefoot walking, heating pads and self-treatment of corns. Lack of pain does not mean an ulcer or infection is harmless.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an organ map connects eyes, kidneys, vessels and nerves; inspect the foot even without pain.

handout.caption: From your guides · Diabetes-related foot changes

topics.title: Neurologic diagnostic studies
topics.recognize: CT identifies acute structural changes; CT angiography examines vessels with iodinated contrast; PET evaluates metabolic activity.
topics.act: Assess contrast history, kidney considerations and procedure preparation; monitor puncture sites or sedation effects when relevant.
topics.remember: Match each test to its purpose. A vascular image, functional metabolic study and bedside neurologic examination answer different questions and complement rather than replace each other.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a camera, vessel map and activity meter represent CT, angiography and PET purposes.

handout.caption: From your guides · CT angiography: nursing care

topics.title: Lumbar puncture and MRI
topics.recognize: Lumbar puncture samples CSF; MRI offers detailed structural imaging using a strong magnetic field.
topics.act: Before LP, review bleeding risk and possible increased-ICP contraindications; afterward monitor headache, leakage and neurologic changes. Before MRI, screen implants/metal and follow device-specific safety rules.
topics.remember: MRI does not use ionizing radiation. Do not assume every implant is safe or prohibited without verifying its exact compatibility.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a CSF sample and magnetic doorway need different preparation and safety checks.

handout.caption: From your guides · Lumbar puncture: nursing care

topics.title: EEG
topics.recognize: An EEG records electrical brain activity and helps classify suspected seizures; a normal interictal tracing does not exclude epilepsy.
topics.act: Prepare according to test instructions and document observed events, medications and possible triggers; protect the patient if a seizure occurs.
topics.remember: EEG studies function rather than brain anatomy. Correlate the tracing with the clinical episode, not the test result alone.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an electrical tracing records brain activity; a quiet strip does not exclude intermittent seizures.

handout.caption: From your guides · EEG: record brain electrical activity

topics.title: Changes in neurologic status
topics.recognize: New confusion, reduced alertness, pupil changes, weakness or speech changes can signal deterioration.
topics.act: Compare with baseline, assess ABCs and glucose, perform focused neurologic checks and report new deficits promptly.
topics.remember: Trend matters: a changing level of consciousness may precede dramatic vital-sign changes. Document onset/last-known-well and avoid assuming sleepiness is simply fatigue or medication effect.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a changing alertness lamp triggers comparison with pupils, movement, speech and baseline.

topics.title: Increased intracranial pressure
covers: Care of the client with increased intracranial pressure
topics.recognize: Declining consciousness, headache, vomiting or pupillary changes suggest raised ICP; late findings can include abnormal posturing and Cushing-pattern vital signs.
topics.act: Maintain oxygenation and perfusion, elevate/align the head as appropriate, avoid obstructing venous return and give ordered ICP therapy.
topics.remember: Prevent secondary injury from hypoxia and hypotension. Do not wait for late bradycardia or abnormal respirations before escalating neurologic deterioration.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a crowded skull squeezes perfusion pipes; alignment and oxygen delivery protect the brain.

topics.title: Head-trauma priorities
covers: Care of the client with head trauma
topics.recognize: Trauma can cause bleeding, edema and evolving neurologic deficits even after an initially reassuring assessment.
topics.act: Protect cervical alignment when indicated, support oxygenation/perfusion and perform serial neurologic assessments; promptly escalate deterioration.
topics.remember: The primary injury has occurred; nursing care aims to prevent secondary injury. Watch consciousness, pupils, motor responses and new vomiting rather than relying only on external wounds.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a damaged helmet hides bleeding; repeated neurologic checks watch for secondary injury.

topics.title: Seizures and status epilepticus
topics.recognize: Observe onset, movements, awareness and recovery. A seizure lasting 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery is an emergency.
topics.act: Time the event, protect from injury, support airway and give prescribed rescue treatment; position safely when possible.
topics.remember: Do not restrain the patient or place objects in the mouth. Afterward assess breathing, injury, glucose and neurologic recovery, and document the sequence.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a seizure stopwatch reaches the emergency mark while soft barriers protect from injury.

topics.title: Migraine
topics.recognize: Migraine often causes episodic throbbing pain with nausea and light/sound sensitivity, sometimes preceded by aura.
topics.act: Reduce stimulation and give prescribed acute treatment early; identify triggers and prevention needs.
topics.remember: A thunderclap headache, fever/stiff neck, new focal deficit or a major change from the usual pattern needs urgent evaluation. Do not label every severe headache a routine migraine.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a familiar migraine dimmer differs from a sudden thunderclap alarm.

topics.title: Transient ischemic attack
topics.recognize: Transient focal weakness, speech or vision changes can reflect temporary cerebral ischemia even after symptoms resolve.
topics.act: Treat as urgent stroke evaluation: note onset, assess deficits and help complete the prescribed vascular/cardiac workup.
topics.remember: Symptom resolution does not remove the near-term stroke risk. TIA is a warning requiring prevention and evaluation, not reassurance alone.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a briefly closed brain gate reopens, but its warning bell still demands urgent evaluation.

handout.caption: From your guides · Stroke — BE FAST and last known well

topics.title: Ischemic stroke
topics.recognize: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech change or other focal deficit suggests interrupted cerebral blood flow.
topics.act: Activate the stroke pathway, establish last-known-well, check glucose and obtain urgent imaging; protect airway and keep NPO until swallowing is assessed.
topics.remember: Reperfusion eligibility depends on imaging, timing and contraindications. Do not give oral medications, food or drink before swallowing safety is established.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a blocked brain pipe starts a last-known-well clock and a swallowing safety gate.

topics.title: Hemorrhagic stroke
topics.recognize: Acute neurologic deficit with severe headache, vomiting or falling consciousness can indicate intracranial bleeding; aneurysmal rupture may cause thunderclap headache.
topics.act: Escalate urgently, support airway/perfusion, control blood pressure as ordered and monitor for rising ICP.
topics.remember: Brain imaging distinguishes hemorrhage from ischemia. Thrombolytic or anticoagulant treatment for presumed ischemia can worsen bleeding if hemorrhage has not been excluded.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a burst brain pipe needs urgent imaging before an ischemic-stroke treatment is assumed.

topics.title: Traumatic brain injury patterns
topics.recognize: Concussion alters brain function. Epidural bleeding can deteriorate rapidly after a lucid interval; subdural bleeding may evolve more slowly; intracerebral bleeding occurs within brain tissue.
topics.act: Protect oxygenation, blood pressure and cervical alignment; repeatedly assess consciousness, pupils and motor findings.
topics.remember: A small external injury or brief initial recovery does not exclude dangerous intracranial bleeding. Prevent secondary injury from hypoxia and hypotension.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a damaged helmet hides bleeding; repeated neurologic checks watch for secondary injury.

topics.title: Primary and metastatic brain tumors
topics.recognize: Primary tumors originate in/near the brain; secondary tumors metastasize from elsewhere. Either can cause seizures, focal deficits or increased ICP.
topics.act: Monitor neurologic changes and implement ordered seizure/edema therapy; after surgery follow location-specific positioning and monitor for deterioration.
topics.remember: Benign does not mean safe inside the skull. Mass, edema and blocked CSF can threaten function regardless of malignancy.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an expanding mass crowds a rigid skull: even a benign growth can raise pressure.

handout.caption: From your guides · Brain tumor: mass and edema

topics.title: Diffuse axonal injury and contusion
topics.recognize: Contusion is bruised brain tissue with focal bleeding/edema. Diffuse axonal injury results from shearing during acceleration/deceleration and may cause prolonged impaired consciousness.
topics.act: Support oxygenation/perfusion, monitor serial neurologic findings and prevent secondary injury.
topics.remember: These differ from a simple concussion. Initial imaging may underestimate diffuse injury, so clinical assessment and trajectory remain essential.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a bruised patch contrasts with stretched connecting wires: contusion versus diffuse axonal injury.

handout.caption: From your guides · Head injury: primary damage and secondary injury

topics.title: Brain death
topics.recognize: Brain death is permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, determined through a formal clinical process.
topics.act: Maintain prescribed physiologic support and clear family communication while qualified clinicians perform required evaluation.
topics.remember: Exclude reversible confounders such as sedatives, hypothermia and metabolic disturbance. Brain death is distinct from coma or a vegetative state; do not infer it from unresponsiveness alone.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a formal checklist separates permanent brain/brainstem failure from reversible unresponsiveness.

topics.title: Spinal cord injury and autonomic emergencies
topics.recognize: Cord injury can impair movement, sensation, breathing and autonomic function. Spinal shock causes transient flaccidity; neurogenic shock causes hypotension/bradycardia; autonomic dysreflexia causes sudden hypertension after susceptible injury.
topics.act: Protect alignment, ventilation and perfusion. For dysreflexia, sit upright, monitor BP and identify triggers, especially bladder distention.
topics.remember: These three conditions are different. A high cord injury creates respiratory and autonomic risks beyond limb weakness.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine three alarms distinguish flaccid spinal shock, low-pressure neurogenic shock and hypertensive dysreflexia.

topics.title: Meningitis versus encephalitis
topics.recognize: Meningitis often causes fever, headache and neck stiffness; encephalitis more directly affects brain function, causing altered behavior, consciousness or seizures.
topics.act: Apply indicated precautions, rapidly escalate neurologic/infection findings and give prescribed antimicrobials/antivirals with supportive care.
topics.remember: Do not delay urgent treatment while awaiting every diagnostic result. Monitor airway, seizures, perfusion and ICP; the organism determines transmission precautions.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an inflamed wrapper causes meningeal signs; an inflamed brain changes behavior and consciousness.

topics.title: Brain abscess
topics.recognize: Localized infection can cause headache, fever, seizures, focal deficits and increased ICP; the full classic pattern may be absent.
topics.act: Arrange urgent evaluation and prescribed antimicrobial or surgical treatment, with seizure and neurologic monitoring.
topics.remember: An intracranial mass changes diagnostic safety. Lumbar puncture may be unsafe when mass effect or raised ICP is suspected; follow the treating team's plan.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an infected pocket occupies skull space and can trigger seizures or focal deficits.

topics.title: Multiple sclerosis
topics.recognize: CNS demyelination can cause fluctuating visual, sensory, motor and coordination problems with fatigue.
topics.act: Balance rest and activity, manage heat sensitivity and mobility risks, and support prescribed relapse/disease-modifying treatment.
topics.remember: Symptoms vary by lesion location and disease course. Avoid overheating and teach strategies that conserve energy without unnecessary long-term immobility.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine damaged insulation interrupts CNS signals; a heat lamp worsens fatigue and symptoms.

topics.title: Myasthenia gravis
topics.recognize: Fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia and difficulty swallowing suggest impaired neuromuscular transmission; weakness worsens with use.
topics.act: Assess breathing and swallowing, schedule medication and meals to optimize strength, and urgently escalate respiratory decline.
topics.remember: A myasthenic crisis threatens ventilation. Do not attribute new dyspnea to ordinary fatigue; medication adherence and avoiding triggers help prevent deterioration.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a muscle battery fades with use; a breathing gauge watches for respiratory weakness.

topics.title: Guillain-Barré syndrome
topics.recognize: Acute progressive weakness, often ascending with reduced reflexes after infection, can involve respiratory and autonomic muscles.
topics.act: Closely monitor respiratory function, swallowing, BP and rhythm; prepare ventilatory support and administer prescribed IVIG or plasma exchange.
topics.remember: Weakness can progress despite an initially normal oxygen saturation. Prevent immobility complications while monitoring for autonomic instability.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine weakness climbs a ladder toward breathing muscles while autonomic gauges fluctuate.

topics.title: Parkinson disease
topics.recognize: Bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability reflect reduced dopamine activity; swallowing and autonomic problems can occur.
topics.act: Give medicines on schedule, support safe mobility, assess swallowing and prevent falls/aspiration.
topics.remember: Timing is part of treatment. Avoid abrupt interruption of antiparkinson medication; use deliberate movements and individualized exercise/communication strategies.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a slow stiff gear needs its medication on schedule and a safe walking path.

topics.title: Bell palsy
topics.recognize: Acute peripheral facial-nerve palsy weakens one side of the face, including forehead movement and eye closure.
topics.act: Protect the exposed cornea with prescribed lubrication/closure measures and arrange prompt evaluation and treatment.
topics.remember: New facial weakness still requires stroke assessment. Bell palsy is a peripheral diagnosis; do not dismiss associated limb weakness, speech changes or other neurologic deficits.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a facial curtain cannot close over the eye; protect the cornea while evaluating the cause.

handout.caption: From your guides · Bell's Palsy Vs Trigeminal

topics.title: Huntington disease
topics.recognize: Inherited neurodegeneration causes involuntary choreiform movements, cognitive decline and psychiatric changes.
topics.act: Support nutrition, swallowing safety, fall prevention and behavioral needs; include family and genetic counseling resources.
topics.remember: Movement, cognition and mood all require assessment. Progressive disability changes supervision and communication needs; preserve dignity and function as long as possible.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine dancing gears and a changing thought board cue movement, cognitive and psychiatric effects.

handout.caption: From your guides · Huntington's disease

topics.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
topics.recognize: Progressive motor-neuron loss causes weakness, muscle wasting, dysarthria and dysphagia, with increasing respiratory risk.
topics.act: Monitor breathing/cough strength and swallowing; support assistive communication, nutrition, mobility and advance-care planning.
topics.remember: Sensory loss is not the defining feature. Cognition is often preserved but cognitive/behavioral changes can occur; do not assume inability to speak means inability to participate.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine motor cables weaken toward a breathing bell while communication tools preserve participation.

handout.caption: From your guides · A.L.S. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis

topics.title: Alzheimer disease
topics.recognize: Progressive memory and functional decline differs from delirium's acute, fluctuating inattention.
topics.act: Use consistent routines, simple cues and safety supports; assess nutrition, wandering and caregiver strain.
topics.remember: A sudden change in someone with dementia needs evaluation for delirium, infection, medication effects or another reversible cause. Do not attribute every acute decline to Alzheimer progression.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a slowly fading memory book differs from delirium's suddenly flickering attention lamp.

topics.title: Degenerative disc disease
topics.recognize: Disc degeneration or herniation can cause back/neck pain with radiating pain, numbness or weakness.
topics.act: Assess motor/sensory function and promote prescribed positioning, activity, analgesia and rehabilitation; after surgery use ordered body mechanics.
topics.remember: New urinary retention, saddle numbness or progressive weakness suggests cauda equina/cord compromise and needs urgent evaluation. Avoid routine prolonged bed rest unless specifically indicated.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a bulging disc presses a nerve; a saddle-and-bladder alarm signals urgent compression.

handout.caption: From your guides · Degenerative disc disease: positioning

topics.title: Basilar skull fracture and CSF leakage
topics.recognize: Periorbital bruising, mastoid bruising or clear ear/nose drainage after head injury can suggest a basilar skull fracture.
topics.act: Protect airway and cervical alignment as indicated; avoid nasal instrumentation and report suspected CSF leakage.
topics.remember: Course recall: a halo/ring pattern and glucose in drainage are clues to possible CSF. Neither alone confirms it; follow definitive evaluation and infection precautions.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a cracked skull base beside a ringed drop: a halo/glucose clue suggests CSF but does not confirm it.

topics.title: Anemia: oxygen-carrying capacity
topics.recognize: Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery, causing fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea or tachycardia; severity depends on onset and the patient's condition.
topics.act: Assess bleeding, perfusion and symptoms; compare CBC indices, reticulocytes and nutrient studies to identify the cause.
topics.remember: Anemia is a finding, not one disease. Treatment differs for blood loss, deficient production and hemolysis; do not apply a transfusion threshold without clinical context.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine too few oxygen delivery trucks prompt a search for loss, poor production or destruction.

handout.caption: From your guides · Anemia: production versus destruction

topics.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
topics.recognize: Small pale red cells, fatigue and pica suggest inadequate iron; chronic blood loss is an important adult cause.
topics.act: Find and address the source of loss and administer prescribed replacement; teach GI effects and correct product use.
topics.remember: Iron treats deficiency but does not explain why it occurred. Dark stools from oral iron differ from suspected gastrointestinal bleeding requiring evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an iron-starved workshop makes small pale cells while a leak inspection finds the cause.

topics.title: Aplastic anemia
topics.recognize: Bone-marrow failure lowers red cells, white cells and platelets, causing fatigue, infection and bleeding risk.
topics.act: Protect against infection and bleeding, monitor CBC trends and urgently report fever; prepare prescribed transfusion or marrow-directed treatment.
topics.remember: Pancytopenia means all three cell lines are reduced. A low neutrophil count can make infection severe even when local inflammatory signs are subtle.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an empty marrow factory loses oxygen trucks, immune guards and platelet patches together.

topics.title: Megaloblastic anemia
topics.recognize: B12 or folate deficiency produces large abnormal cells. B12 deficiency can also cause paresthesias, balance problems and cognitive changes.
topics.act: Check the cause and replace the missing nutrient as prescribed; assess neurologic findings and nutrition/absorption history.
topics.remember: Folate can improve blood counts while untreated B12-related neurologic injury continues. Distinguish the deficiencies rather than choosing replacement from cell size alone.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine oversized red cells beside a tingling glove: B12 deficiency adds neurologic findings.

topics.title: Erythropoietin
topics.recognize: Epoetin stimulates marrow red-cell production in selected anemias; response requires adequate iron and monitoring.
topics.act: Trend hemoglobin and blood pressure, assess iron status and follow individualized dosing.
topics.remember: The goal is to reduce transfusion need in appropriate patients, not normalize every hemoglobin. Excessive targets can increase cardiovascular/thrombotic risk; benefit is delayed rather than immediate rescue.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a marrow production signal beside a blood-pressure gauge: epoetin stimulates cells but needs monitoring.

topics.title: Sickle-cell disease
topics.recognize: Sickled cells hemolyze and obstruct small vessels, causing anemia, jaundice and painful vaso-occlusive episodes.
topics.act: Assess pain, hydration and oxygenation; give prescribed analgesia and fluids. New chest pain, fever or breathing difficulty needs urgent acute-chest evaluation.
topics.remember: Prevent hypoxia, dehydration and infection. Oxygen is indicated for hypoxemia, not automatically for every pain episode; avoid both dehydration and fluid overload.

topics.title: Polycythemia vera
topics.recognize: Excess red cells increase blood viscosity; headache, ruddy color, itching after bathing and thrombosis can occur.
topics.act: Monitor clot/bleeding symptoms and follow prescribed phlebotomy or cytoreductive treatment; support hydration as appropriate.
topics.remember: This is excessive cell production, not simply dehydration. New focal deficits, chest pain or dyspnea require urgent assessment for vascular complications.

topics.title: AML, CML, ALL and CLL
topics.recognize: Leukemia crowds marrow, causing infection, anemia and bleeding despite potentially high WBC. Acute types involve immature blasts; chronic types usually progress more slowly.
topics.act: Trend CBC/differential, assess fever/bleeding and support type-specific diagnostic and treatment plans.
topics.remember: AML is myeloid and often adult; CML involves BCR-ABL; ALL is lymphoid and affects children and adults; CLL generally affects older adults. Names encode lineage and tempo.

topics.title: Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin lymphoma
topics.recognize: Painless lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats or weight loss may signal lymphoma.
topics.act: Arrange diagnostic follow-up, monitor treatment-related infection risk and assess symptoms suggesting organ or airway compression.
topics.remember: Hodgkin lymphoma classically has Reed-Sternberg cells and more orderly spread; non-Hodgkin includes many diverse lymphoid cancers and can involve extranodal sites. Tissue diagnosis determines classification.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a lymph-node station compares Reed-Sternberg clues with diverse non-Hodgkin routes.

topics.title: Multiple myeloma
topics.recognize: Malignant plasma cells can cause bone pain/fractures, hypercalcemia, kidney injury, anemia and infection risk.
topics.act: Protect fragile bones, monitor renal function/calcium and maintain prescribed hydration and treatment.
topics.remember: CRAB: Calcium elevation, Renal injury, Anemia, Bone lesions. A monoclonal protein supports evaluation; back pain or weakness needs assessment for fracture or spinal compression.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a plasma-cell stamp cracks bones beside a calcium pile, kidney alarm and anemia truck.

topics.title: Low platelets: ITP versus HIT
topics.recognize: Thrombocytopenia commonly causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding. ITP is immune platelet destruction; HIT is a heparin-associated immune reaction with major clot risk.
topics.act: Assess bleeding and platelet trend, protect from injury and report suspected HIT promptly for stopping all heparin and prescribed non-heparin therapy.
topics.remember: A falling count on heparin is not just bleeding risk. Treatment depends on the cause, not the number alone.

topics.title: Hemophilia
topics.recognize: Clotting-factor deficiency causes deep tissue or joint bleeding; platelet count may be normal.
topics.act: Protect the affected joint, administer prescribed factor replacement and coordinate invasive procedures with the bleeding-disorders plan.
topics.remember: Hemophilia A involves factor VIII; B involves factor IX. Deep bleeding points toward factor failure, whereas platelet disorders more often cause petechiae and mucosal bleeding.

topics.title: von Willebrand disease
topics.recognize: Reduced or abnormal von Willebrand factor impairs platelet adhesion and factor VIII support, producing nose/gum bleeding, heavy menses or procedural bleeding.
topics.act: Assess bleeding history, avoid unapproved platelet-impairing drugs and follow the prescribed desmopressin/factor plan.
topics.remember: It affects people of any sex and often produces mucosal bleeding. Do not assume a normal platelet count excludes a bleeding disorder.

topics.title: DIC
topics.recognize: Widespread coagulation consumes platelets/factors, causing microvascular clots, organ dysfunction and bleeding such as IV-site oozing.
topics.act: Urgently treat the trigger and monitor perfusion, bleeding, platelets, coagulation tests and fibrinogen; give blood components or anticoagulation only as directed for the presentation.
topics.remember: DIC combines clotting and bleeding. Treatment priorities change with the underlying illness and whether bleeding or thrombosis dominates.

topics.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
topics.recognize: Platelet-rich microthrombi cause thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia, with possible neurologic or kidney injury.
topics.act: Escalate urgently for specialist treatment such as plasma exchange; monitor organ function and bleeding.
topics.remember: Do not wait for the full classic symptom pentad. TTP differs from DIC and HIT; routine platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless a specialist identifies a critical indication.

topics.title: Blood products and compatibility
topics.recognize: Packed red cells improve oxygen-carrying capacity; platelets support the initial plug; fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors.
topics.act: Verify patient/product identity, prescription, compatibility and baseline status; use the facility administration/monitoring procedure.
topics.remember: Compatibility depends on the component: red-cell antigens versus plasma antibodies. Blood products treat specific deficits; do not use one universal donor/recipient rule for every product.

topics.title: Early transfusion-reaction clues
covers: Transfusion reactions including manifestations and medical and nursing management.
topics.recognize: Acute hemolysis can cause fever, flank pain, hypotension or dark urine. Febrile reactions cause fever/rigors; allergic reactions often cause hives/itching.
topics.act: For any suspected reaction, stop the transfusion, assess ABCs, maintain access per protocol and notify the provider/transfusion service.
topics.remember: Fever is not automatically benign: hemolysis and contamination must be excluded. Never restart a suspect unit without explicit direction.

topics.title: TACO
topics.recognize: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload causes respiratory distress with signs of excess volume, often hypertension, crackles and neck-vein distention.
topics.act: Stop the transfusion, sit upright as appropriate, support oxygenation and give ordered overload treatment; monitor fluid balance.
topics.remember: TACO is a volume problem. Slower/smaller-volume transfusion plans may help susceptible patients; avoid reflexively giving a fluid bolus for every transfusion reaction.

topics.title: TRALI
topics.recognize: Transfusion-related acute lung injury causes acute hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary edema without circulatory overload; hypotension can occur.
topics.act: Stop the transfusion, summon help and provide respiratory/hemodynamic support according to the reaction protocol.
topics.remember: Both TRALI and TACO can produce wet lungs. Look for evidence of overload rather than deciding solely from crackles; diuresis is not a universal reaction treatment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a lung barrier becomes leaky without an overflowing tank: TRALI is not simple volume overload.

topics.title: Bacterial transfusion reaction
topics.recognize: High fever, rigors, hypotension or shock during/after transfusion can indicate a contaminated component.
topics.act: Stop the transfusion, support ABCs and notify the provider/blood bank; prepare cultures of the patient/component and prescribed urgent antibiotics.
topics.remember: Severe fever is not automatically a simple febrile reaction. Preserve the bag/tubing for investigation according to facility policy.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a contaminated blood bag triggers fever and shock alarms requiring immediate response.
