topics.title: Cancer basics, diagnosis and staging
covers: Cancer management: Medical, surgical, and nursing management
topics.recognize: Carcinogenic exposures and genetic changes promote abnormal growth. Persistent lumps, bleeding, weight loss or other changes require evaluation; biopsy establishes many diagnoses.
topics.act: Assess warning signs, support diagnostic testing and coordinate individualized surgery, systemic treatment, radiation and symptom care.
topics.remember: Stage describes extent/spread; grade describes microscopic abnormality. Treatment goals may be curative, controlling or palliative; cancer is not one uniform disease.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a growth map measures spread while a microscope grades cell abnormality.

handout.caption: From your guides · Cancer prevention and early detection

topics.title: Cancer types and immune surveillance
topics.recognize: Immune surveillance can remove abnormal cells, but tumors can evade it. Carcinoma is epithelial, sarcoma connective tissue, leukemia blood-forming, lymphoma lymphoid and myeloma plasma-cell disease.
topics.act: Support type-specific treatment and survivorship monitoring, rehabilitation and recurrence prevention.
topics.remember: Tertiary prevention reduces consequences after disease exists. Immunotherapy redirects immune activity and has distinct adverse effects; it is not interchangeable with cytotoxic chemotherapy.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine different cancer family branches evade immune guards; survivorship repairs later consequences.

topics.title: Primary versus secondary prevention
topics.recognize: Primary prevention reduces cancer risk before disease: avoid tobacco, protect skin and use indicated vaccination. Secondary prevention detects disease earlier through appropriate screening.
topics.act: Match screening to age, history, risk and current guidelines; help complete abnormal-result follow-up.
topics.remember: Screening examines people without symptoms; diagnostic testing investigates a finding. An abnormal screen is not itself a confirmed cancer diagnosis.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a prevention shield stops risk before disease; a screening lantern seeks early disease.

topics.title: External radiation versus brachytherapy
topics.recognize: Radiation injury depends on the treated tissue and can cause local skin/mucosal effects and fatigue. External-beam treatment does not make the person radioactive; some internal sources require precautions.
topics.act: Follow the specific source's time, distance, shielding and visitor rules; protect treated skin and report toxicity.
topics.remember: For a displaced sealed source, restrict access and notify radiation safety; never pick it up by hand. Restrictions depend on the actual treatment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an outside beam and an inside source have different radiation-safety boundaries.

handout.caption: From your guides · Brachytherapy · Nursing picture guide

topics.title: Chemotherapy administration and staff protection
topics.recognize: Cytotoxic therapy affects rapidly dividing cancer and normal cells; adverse effects vary by agent and dose.
topics.act: Verify regimen, access, labs and required checks; use hazardous-drug PPE/handling and disposal procedures, and assess patient-specific toxicities.
topics.remember: Precautions include exposure during preparation, administration, waste and body-fluid handling according to protocol. Do not assume all anticancer drugs share the same route, timing or toxicity.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a labeled hazardous-drug station checks the regimen and protects both patient and staff.

topics.title: Chemotherapy extravasation
topics.recognize: Burning, pain, swelling or altered infusion flow can signal drug leaking into tissue; vesicants can cause major injury.
topics.act: Stop infusion immediately, keep access available for aspiration/antidote per protocol and notify the treatment team; do not flush the suspected site.
topics.remember: Antidote and warm/cold compress choice depend on the drug. Follow the agent-specific extravasation plan rather than applying one compress rule to every medication.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a leaking infusion pipe meets a stop sign: stop and follow the drug-specific plan; do not flush.

handout.caption: From your guides · IV site findings: infiltration versus phlebitis

topics.title: Nausea, mouth injury and cancer nutrition
topics.recognize: Chemotherapy-related nausea/vomiting and mucositis/stomatitis can reduce intake and damage the oral barrier.
topics.act: Give prescribed preventive antiemetics, provide gentle oral care and bland rinses, manage pain and adapt foods/fluids to tolerance.
topics.remember: Monitor dehydration, weight and infection. Avoid irritating alcohol-containing rinses or abrasive foods when mucosa is injured; nutrition support should fit symptoms and the overall care plan.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a sore mouth guards a food tray: gentle care, antiemetics and pain relief support intake.

handout.caption: From your guides · Oral mucositis in children

topics.title: Bone-marrow suppression
topics.recognize: Low neutrophils increase infection risk, low platelets bleeding risk and low red cells fatigue/dyspnea.
topics.act: Trend CBC/differential, teach urgent fever reporting and appropriate infection/bleeding precautions; assess activity tolerance and prescribed support.
topics.remember: A high total WBC does not ensure functional immunity. Positive-pressure rooms are not routine for every low white count; protective environments have specific indications.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a quiet factory loses immune guards, platelet patches and oxygen trucks after treatment.

topics.title: Chemotherapy organ toxicities
topics.recognize: Renal injury changes urine/kidney labs; neurotoxicity/peripheral neuropathy causes numbness or weakness; cardiopulmonary injury can cause dyspnea/chest symptoms. Reproductive effects include fertility and pregnancy risks; fatigue is common.
topics.act: Trend agent-specific monitoring, assess falls and function, report new symptoms and teach contraception/fertility guidance before therapy.
topics.remember: Do not dismiss breathlessness as ordinary fatigue. Toxicity monitoring depends on the actual drug and cumulative exposure.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine kidney, nerve, heart/lung and fertility gauges track drug-specific toxicities.

topics.title: Cancer pain
topics.recognize: Cancer pain may be somatic, visceral or neuropathic and may include breakthrough episodes despite baseline treatment.
topics.act: Assess intensity, function and patient goals; use scheduled and breakthrough medication as ordered, with nonpharmacologic support and reassessment.
topics.remember: Monitor sedation, respirations, constipation and other adverse effects. Effective pain relief is individualized; opioid tolerance does not eliminate monitoring needs or justify withholding relief.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a scheduled comfort clock and breakthrough bell guide individualized pain relief.

handout.caption: From your guides · Pain Management Detailed

topics.title: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation
topics.recognize: Conditioning and delayed marrow recovery create infection, bleeding and organ-toxicity risks. Allogeneic transplant adds graft-versus-host disease risk.
topics.act: Monitor engraftment/counts, temperature, mucosa, skin, GI and liver findings; follow transplant-specific precautions and immunosuppressive therapy.
topics.remember: Autologous uses the patient's cells; allogeneic uses donor cells. New rash, diarrhea or jaundice after donor transplant needs prompt evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a new marrow garden needs protection while donor cells may challenge host tissues.

topics.title: Four oncologic emergencies
topics.recognize: SVC: face/neck swelling and dyspnea. Tumor lysis: high potassium/phosphate/uric acid and low calcium. Spinal compression: new back pain, weakness or bladder/bowel changes. Hypercalcemia: weakness, confusion and dehydration.
topics.act: Escalate immediately; support ABCs and prepare ordered targeted treatment, ECG/lab monitoring or urgent imaging.
topics.remember: The pattern identifies the threat. New neurologic deficits or breathing compromise cannot wait for a routine oncology appointment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine four bells mark swollen face, lysed cells, compressed cord and high calcium.

handout.caption: From your guides · Blood and cancer-related signs

topics.title: Palliative, hospice and end-of-life care
topics.recognize: Serious illness creates physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs alongside disease management.
topics.act: Ask what matters to the patient, treat distressing symptoms and support family/communication and advance-care planning.
topics.remember: Palliative care can accompany disease-directed treatment at any stage. Hospice is a particular end-of-life model with eligibility requirements; neither means abandoning symptom treatment or the patient.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine helping hands hold comfort beside treatment; palliative support can accompany disease-directed care.

topics.title: Female reproductive assessment and breast awareness
topics.recognize: Assess bleeding pattern, pelvic symptoms, sexual/reproductive history and new breast changes while maintaining consent and privacy.
topics.act: Report a new lump, nipple/skin change or unusual discharge; arrange appropriate clinical assessment and indicated screening.
topics.remember: Breast self-awareness complements screening but does not replace mammography or diagnostic evaluation. Do not use a normal self-exam to dismiss persistent symptoms.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a private assessment doorway protects dignity while new symptoms receive evaluation.

handout.caption: From your guides · Breast changes to recognize

topics.title: Reproductive screening and biopsy
covers: Pelvic exam with Pap and HPV
topics.recognize: Pap testing examines cervical cells; HPV testing detects high-risk viral infection. Pelvic examination assesses anatomy; colposcopy magnifies the cervix, while cervical/endometrial biopsy samples tissue.
topics.act: Explain consent/preparation and aftercare; investigate abnormal bleeding or positive screening through the prescribed pathway.
topics.remember: Screening intervals depend on age, history and current guidelines. Pap tests do not screen reliably for ovarian or endometrial cancer.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a cell sample, virus test and tissue biopsy answer different reproductive questions.

handout.caption: From your guides · Pelvic exam with Pap and HPV test

topics.title: Hysterosalpingogram
topics.recognize: Contrast imaging outlines the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes, commonly during infertility evaluation.
topics.act: Confirm pregnancy exclusion, infection symptoms and contrast-reaction history; follow scheduling/preparation instructions and teach postprocedure warning signs.
topics.remember: Usually scheduled after menstruation and before expected ovulation. Mild cramping may occur; fever, severe pain or heavy bleeding needs prompt reporting.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine contrast traces the uterine room and fallopian passageways after pregnancy is excluded.

handout.caption: From your guides · Hysterosalpingogram

topics.title: Cystocele versus rectocele
topics.recognize: Cystocele is bladder prolapse into the anterior vaginal wall, often affecting urination; rectocele involves rectal bulging into the posterior wall and can affect defecation.
topics.act: Assess emptying, discomfort and tissue integrity; support prescribed pelvic-floor therapy, pessary care or surgery.
topics.remember: Distinguish the organ involved. Prevent constipation/straining and report retention or compromised tissue rather than treating every bulge as the same disorder.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a front bladder bulge differs from a back rectal bulge in the vaginal wall.

handout.caption: From your guides · Cystocele and rectocele

topics.title: Fibrocystic breast changes
topics.recognize: Benign breast changes may cause cyclic tenderness and nodularity that vary with menstruation.
topics.act: Assess the pattern and arrange evaluation of new, persistent or focal abnormalities; provide prescribed comfort measures.
topics.remember: Cyclic symptoms can support a benign pattern but do not prove it. A new discrete lump or concerning skin/nipple change still needs assessment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a monthly tenderness clock suggests cyclic changes, but a new fixed lump gets checked.

handout.caption: From your guides · Breast ultrasound and cyst aspiration

topics.title: Breast cancer and management
topics.recognize: A new persistent lump, skin dimpling, nipple retraction/discharge or other change warrants evaluation; mammography detects findings that may need biopsy.
topics.act: Support diagnostic follow-up and individualized surgery, radiation, endocrine, targeted or systemic treatment; after surgery monitor wounds, drains, movement and lymphedema risk.
topics.remember: Treatment depends on stage and tumor receptors. Screening and diagnostic mammography have different purposes; absence of pain does not exclude cancer.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a new breast change lights a diagnostic path; receptors and stage guide treatment choices.

topics.title: Ovarian and endometrial cancer
topics.recognize: Ovarian cancer can present with persistent bloating, early satiety and pelvic symptoms. Endometrial cancer commonly causes abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding.
topics.act: Escalate persistent symptoms and support appropriate imaging/tissue diagnosis and specialist treatment.
topics.remember: There is no routine Pap-based ovarian screening. Postmenopausal bleeding needs evaluation even when small; do not dismiss it as normal aging.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine persistent bloating and a postmenopausal bleeding bell identify different gynecologic warnings.

topics.title: Bacterial STIs and PID
topics.recognize: Chlamydia and gonorrhea may be silent but can cause cervicitis, ascending PID and infertility. Syphilis progresses through stages and may include a painless chancre.
topics.act: Arrange testing, prescribed antibiotics, partner management and follow-up; assess pelvic pain/fever urgently for PID.
topics.remember: Treat partners and follow abstinence instructions to prevent reinfection. A positive test or absent symptoms does not define the stage or exclude complications.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine bacterial footprints climb toward the pelvis: targeted antibiotics and partner care prevent complications.

handout.caption: From your guides · STIs — Visual Study Guide

topics.title: HPV and genital herpes
topics.recognize: HPV can cause warts and oncogenic infection; herpes produces recurrent painful lesions but can transmit without visible lesions.
topics.act: Teach vaccination/screening where appropriate, safer sex and prescribed antiviral care; assess pregnancy-related implications.
topics.remember: Antibiotics do not eradicate these viruses. HPV prevention includes vaccination and cervical screening; herpes antivirals suppress symptoms and transmission risk but do not cure infection.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine two viral stamps need prevention and symptom control; antibiotics cannot erase them.

handout.caption: From your guides · STI — Gonorrhea, HSV & HPV

topics.title: Syphilis and trichomoniasis
topics.recognize: Syphilis can cause painless ulceration and later systemic disease; trichomoniasis may cause genital irritation/discharge or no symptoms.
topics.act: Use organism-specific testing and prescribed treatment, coordinate partner treatment and follow-up, and teach reinfection prevention.
topics.remember: Syphilis is bacterial; trichomoniasis is protozoal. Do not choose therapy from discharge appearance alone or assume symptoms must be present for transmission.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a bacterium and a protozoan wear different labels: test and choose organism-specific therapy.

handout.caption: From your guides · STI treatments & post-exposure prevention

topics.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
topics.recognize: Irregular ovulation, hyperandrogenic features and metabolic risk can occur; ultrasound appearance alone does not establish PCOS.
topics.act: Assess menstrual, fertility and metabolic concerns, support individualized lifestyle/medication treatment and monitor abnormal bleeding.
topics.remember: PCOS links reproductive and metabolic health. Treatment differs depending on pregnancy goals; endometrial protection matters when prolonged anovulation occurs.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an irregular ovulation clock connects androgen clues with a metabolic scale.

handout.caption: From your guides · PCOS symptoms

topics.title: Uterine fibroids
topics.recognize: Benign uterine smooth-muscle tumors can cause heavy bleeding, pressure, pain or fertility concerns; some are asymptomatic.
topics.act: Assess bleeding/anemia and symptom burden; explain observation, medication or procedural options based on goals and findings.
topics.remember: Fibroids are not automatically malignant. Location, size, symptoms and future fertility affect management; acute severe bleeding needs prompt stabilization.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine benign muscle knots crowd the uterus and can increase bleeding or pressure.

handout.caption: From your guides · Uterine fibroids

topics.title: Hysterectomy
topics.recognize: Removal of the uterus ends uterine bleeding and the ability to carry a pregnancy; ovarian hormone effects depend on whether ovaries are removed.
topics.act: Monitor postoperative bleeding, pain, bladder/bowel function and thromboembolism risk; teach procedure-specific activity and follow-up.
topics.remember: Hysterectomy does not automatically mean both ovaries were removed. Address sexual, reproductive and emotional concerns without assuming every patient has the same priorities.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a removed uterine room leaves a separate ovarian switch: hormone effects depend on ovary removal.

handout.caption: From your guides · Hysterectomy: surgical approaches

topics.title: Menstrual disorders and endometriosis
topics.recognize: Abnormal bleeding, amenorrhea or disabling cramps require evaluation. Endometriosis involves endometrium-like tissue outside the uterus and can cause cyclic pain, dyspareunia and infertility.
topics.act: Assess pregnancy possibility, bleeding/anemia and function; support prescribed analgesic, hormonal or surgical treatment.
topics.remember: Pain severity does not reliably indicate endometriosis stage. Do not normalize heavy bleeding or severe pain that disrupts daily activity.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine cyclic pain appears outside the uterine room: endometriosis can affect function and fertility.

handout.caption: From your guides · Endometriosis

topics.title: Perimenopause and hormone therapy
topics.recognize: Changing ovarian function can cause irregular cycles, vasomotor symptoms, sleep disruption and genitourinary symptoms.
topics.act: Discuss symptom goals and individualized hormonal/nonhormonal options, considering contraindications and bleeding history.
topics.remember: Menopausal hormone therapy is not contraception. Systemic estrogen generally requires endometrial protection when the uterus is present; new postmenopausal bleeding still needs evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an irregular hormone clock needs symptom-specific care; treatment does not equal contraception.

handout.caption: From your guides · Menopause: symptoms and physical changes

topics.title: Male reproductive assessment
topics.recognize: Urinary symptoms, genital pain, sexual concerns or a new mass need a respectful, focused history and examination.
topics.act: Maintain privacy, use clear nonjudgmental questions and urgently escalate acute retention, severe testicular pain or systemic infection findings.
topics.remember: Age does not make every symptom benign. Differentiate obstruction, inflammation, vascular problems and malignancy rather than assuming all symptoms arise from prostate enlargement.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a private assessment door separates obstruction, infection, vascular symptoms and new masses.

handout.caption: From your guides · Male reproductive anatomy

topics.title: Prostate cancer, PSA and DRE
topics.recognize: Early prostate cancer may be asymptomatic; PSA and digital rectal examination can identify findings requiring further evaluation.
topics.act: Support shared decisions about screening and explain follow-up testing/biopsy and individualized treatment.
topics.remember: PSA is not cancer-specific and can rise with benign conditions. A high PSA or abnormal DRE prompts evaluation rather than confirming cancer by itself.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a PSA flag and examination point toward evaluation, not an automatic cancer verdict.

topics.title: EPCA-2
topics.recognize: EPCA-2 appears in course diagnostic terminology as a proposed prostate-cancer biomarker.
topics.act: Recognize the term, but use current clinician-directed screening and diagnostic pathways.
topics.remember: The linked course clarification identifies EPCA-2 as investigational rather than a routine recommended screening test. Distinguish historical/research terminology from a test actually ordered in present clinical practice.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an EPCA-2 label stays on a research shelf rather than a routine screening checklist.

handout.caption: From your guides · Prostate vs testicular — screening is different

topics.title: Male reproductive diagnostic tests
covers: Culture and sensitivity of prostatic fluid
topics.recognize: TRUS images the prostate and can guide biopsy; penile Doppler assesses vascular contributions to erectile dysfunction; cultures evaluate suspected infection.
topics.act: Explain test-specific preparation/aftercare and monitor bleeding, fever or worsening symptoms after invasive procedures.
topics.remember: Prostatic massage/culture procedures are inappropriate in suspected acute bacterial prostatitis because of bacteremia risk. Match the diagnostic procedure to the clinical question.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an ultrasound map, blood-flow gauge and culture dish answer different diagnostic questions.

topics.title: BPH and TURP
topics.recognize: Benign prostate enlargement can cause hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying and retention.
topics.act: Assess bladder distention and renal effects; after TURP maintain ordered catheter/irrigation flow and monitor urine, bleeding, pain and fluid balance.
topics.remember: If irrigation is used, subtract irrigant from total drainage to estimate urine output. New obstruction, heavy bleeding or systemic deterioration needs prompt evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an enlarged prostate narrows an outlet; irrigation input must be subtracted from drainage.

topics.title: Erectile dysfunction
topics.recognize: Difficulty achieving/maintaining erection may reflect vascular, neurologic, medication, hormonal or psychological factors.
topics.act: Assess contributing conditions and medications, support confidential discussion and prescribed treatment.
topics.remember: PDE-5 inhibitors must not be combined with nitrates because profound hypotension can occur. Erectile dysfunction can be a vascular-health clue, not simply an inevitable effect of aging.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a vascular-flow key carries a nitrate warning: the medication combination can collapse pressure.

handout.caption: From your guides · Erectile Dysfunction Drugs

topics.title: Prostatitis
topics.recognize: Pelvic/perineal pain and urinary symptoms suggest prostatic inflammation; fever and systemic illness raise concern for acute bacterial infection.
topics.act: Obtain ordered cultures and antibiotics, monitor retention/sepsis and provide prescribed comfort measures.
topics.remember: Avoid prostate massage with acute bacterial prostatitis. Chronic pelvic pain syndromes are not always bacterial and do not all require the same antibiotic approach.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an inflamed prostate sounds a fever alarm; massage can spread acute bacterial infection.

topics.title: Epididymitis
topics.recognize: Inflammation causes scrotal pain/swelling, sometimes with urinary symptoms or fever; causes vary with STI and urinary-tract risks.
topics.act: Arrange evaluation, prescribed antimicrobials and supportive measures such as scrotal support and analgesia.
topics.remember: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain requires urgent assessment for torsion. Do not delay a time-critical torsion evaluation by assuming all scrotal pain is infection.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a painful scrotal pathway needs infection evaluation while torsion starts an urgent clock.

handout.caption: From your guides · Epididymitis

topics.title: Testicular cancer
topics.recognize: A painless testicular lump, enlargement or heaviness can indicate malignancy, often in younger adults.
topics.act: Promptly refer new findings for examination and ultrasound; discuss fertility preservation before treatments that may affect reproduction.
topics.remember: Pain may be absent. A new mass is not diagnosed by self-exam alone and should not be watched indefinitely without evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a painless new testicular lump opens an evaluation gate rather than a wait-and-see clock.

topics.title: Emergency nursing priorities
topics.recognize: Emergency patients can deteriorate rapidly; airway, breathing, hemorrhage and perfusion threats take priority over a complete history.
topics.act: Use a systematic primary survey, treat life threats as found and reassess after each intervention; complete the secondary survey once stabilized.
topics.remember: Triage determines urgency, not diagnosis. A patient initially classified as lower acuity needs reassessment if symptoms or vital signs change.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an ABCDE doorway treats threats before the full history is collected.

topics.title: Scope, law and sentinel events
topics.recognize: Nurse Practice Acts/board rules define scope; competence, delegation and policy further limit assignments. Sentinel events meet serious patient-safety criteria.
topics.act: Stabilize the patient, document facts, report through the safety/command process and request qualified help for tasks outside competence.
topics.remember: A disaster does not automatically waive licensure or authorize unfamiliar invasive procedures. Safety review seeks system improvement rather than concealment or blame.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a scope boundary and incident-command sign guide safe emergency duties and reporting.

topics.title: Routine versus disaster triage
covers: Disaster triage and the nurse’s role
topics.recognize: Routine triage prioritizes the sickest; mass-casualty triage allocates limited resources to maximize survivable benefit.
topics.act: Use the designated algorithm, tag/document and repeatedly reassess. Adult START uses walking, breathing, perfusion and ability to follow commands.
topics.remember: Red is immediate, yellow delayed and green minor; black designation follows the algorithm's deceased/expectant definitions. Do not mix adult START thresholds with pediatric or other systems.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine colored triage doors allocate urgency and open again for reassessment.

handout.caption: From your guides · Adult START disaster triage

topics.title: Primary ABCDE and secondary survey
topics.recognize: Airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure identify immediate threats; catastrophic external bleeding may take precedence in the trauma protocol.
topics.act: Protect the cervical spine when indicated, treat threats immediately, prevent hypothermia and repeat the survey.
topics.remember: The secondary survey adds history and head-to-toe assessment after immediate threats are addressed. Do not finish a checklist while an identified life threat remains untreated.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine aBCDE stations address threats first; the secondary-survey notebook follows stabilization.

handout.caption: From your guides · Primary survey ABCDE

topics.title: Multiple trauma and abdominal injury
topics.recognize: Shock or occult internal bleeding can occur despite limited external findings or an initially normal hemoglobin.
topics.act: Control hemorrhage, support oxygenation/perfusion and spinal precautions as indicated; trend mental status, urine, abdominal findings and labs. Prepare FAST/CT or surgery according to stability.
topics.remember: Keep NPO and support impaled objects in place. Mechanism and repeated assessment matter; one normal early result cannot exclude bleeding.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an intact outer wall can hide abdominal bleeding; serial perfusion checks search inside.

topics.title: Wound cleaning and closure
topics.recognize: Depth, contamination, tissue viability, mechanism and time influence wound management.
topics.act: Control bleeding, assess neurovascular status, clean/irrigate as ordered and evaluate foreign bodies and tetanus needs.
topics.remember: Primary closure closes a suitable wound promptly; delayed primary closure waits while contamination/infection risk is managed. Do not close every contaminated wound immediately or use an arbitrary universal time cutoff.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a cleaning station sends suitable wounds to closure and contaminated wounds to reassessment.

handout.caption: From your guides · Wound Care

topics.title: Tetanus prophylaxis
topics.recognize: Risk depends on wound characteristics and vaccination history, not simply whether an object was rusty.
topics.act: Clean the wound, verify documented immunization and arrange vaccine and tetanus immune globulin when indicated by the current wound algorithm.
topics.remember: A booster and immune globulin serve different functions. Dirty/major wounds and incomplete or unknown vaccine histories require different decisions from clean minor wounds with complete protection.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a wound tag and vaccine record together select booster and immune-globulin needs.

topics.title: Chest-tube safety
topics.recognize: Assess respiratory status and drainage function; persistent water-seal bubbling can suggest an air leak.
topics.act: Keep the system closed, unobstructed and below chest level. For distress, disconnection or dislodgement, assess the patient and summon help under the emergency protocol.
topics.remember: Do not routinely clamp a bubbling chest tube. Intermittent bubbling while air evacuates differs from persistent leakage.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a closed drain stays below the chest while persistent bubbling signals a possible leak.

handout.caption: From your guides · Chest Tubes — the three chambers

topics.title: Crush injury
topics.recognize: Damaged muscle releases potassium and myoglobin, risking dysrhythmias, shock, compartment syndrome and acute kidney injury.
topics.act: Coordinate safe extrication and early prescribed resuscitation; monitor ECG, potassium, kidney function, urine, CK and limb perfusion.
topics.remember: The threat is systemic as well as local. Hyperkalemia or compartment syndrome needs urgent treatment rather than waiting for visible skin damage to worsen.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine crushed muscle releases potassium and myoglobin toward the heart and kidneys.

handout.caption: From your guides · Rhabdomyolysis

topics.title: Heatstroke, hypothermia and frostbite
topics.recognize: Heatstroke causes hyperthermia with neurologic dysfunction; hypothermia impairs circulation/mental status; frostbite freezes local tissue.
topics.act: Heatstroke: rapid cooling and ABC support. Hypothermia: handle gently and rewarm as directed. Frostbite: protect tissue and use controlled rewarming only when refreezing can be prevented.
topics.remember: Do not rub frostbitten tissue. Sweating can still occur in heatstroke; altered mental status is a critical clue.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a heat alarm needs cooling; a frozen tissue sign needs protected controlled rewarming.

handout.caption: From your guides · Hyperthermia: clinical overview

topics.title: Poisoning and overdose
topics.recognize: Substances can impair breathing, circulation, consciousness or organs; identify agent, dose, route and timing when possible.
topics.act: Protect responders, support ABCs, contact toxicology/Poison Control and give ordered agent-specific treatment.
topics.remember: Do not routinely induce vomiting or give activated charcoal to everyone. Charcoal has limited indications and is unsafe with an unprotected airway; antidotes depend on the toxin.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a labeled poison bottle points to ABC support and its specific treatment, not a universal antidote.

handout.caption: From your guides · Toxic Ranges & Antidotes 2

topics.title: Carbon-monoxide poisoning
topics.recognize: Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or collapse after combustion exposure suggest CO toxicity; several affected people strengthen suspicion.
topics.act: Move to a safe environment, give indicated high-concentration oxygen and arrange urgent evaluation with appropriate co-oximetry and specialist guidance.
topics.remember: Conventional pulse oximetry can appear normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin. Do not use that reading to rule out poisoning.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine invisible gas occupies oxygen seats while a normal-looking pulse-ox light gives false reassurance.

handout.caption: From your guides · Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (Simple Nursing)

topics.title: Food poisoning
topics.recognize: Food exposure followed by vomiting/diarrhea suggests toxin or infection; assess dehydration, bloody stool, fever and high-risk host factors.
topics.act: Restore fluids/electrolytes, obtain indicated testing and use appropriate infection precautions; report suspected clusters.
topics.remember: Not every case requires antibiotics or antimotility drugs. Neurologic symptoms, severe illness or inability to maintain fluids requires urgent reassessment.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an unsafe meal spills a fluid tank; hydration and outbreak assessment guide care.

handout.caption: From your guides · Infectious gastroenteritis

topics.title: Acute alcohol intoxication
topics.recognize: Alcohol can depress consciousness and breathing, but trauma, hypoglycemia or co-ingestion may produce similar findings.
topics.act: Protect airway, check glucose, assess injuries and monitor vital signs; provide prescribed supportive care and watch for evolving withdrawal.
topics.remember: Do not dismiss reduced consciousness as intoxication without assessment. Safety, aspiration prevention and a nonjudgmental approach come before social conclusions.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a sleepy brain sits beside glucose and injury checks: never assume alcohol explains every change.

handout.caption: From your guides · Alchol Abuse

topics.title: Snakebite
topics.recognize: Envenomation can produce local swelling/pain, coagulopathy, neurologic findings or shock; effects depend on the snake.
topics.act: Keep the patient calm, limit limb movement, remove constricting items and arrange urgent evaluation/antivenom when indicated.
topics.remember: Do not cut, suck, ice or apply a constricting tourniquet to the bite. Avoid attempts to capture the snake that create another exposure.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a still protected limb moves toward urgent care, away from cutting, suction and tourniquets.

topics.title: Assault, trafficking and psychiatric safety
topics.recognize: Injury, fear, controlling companions or inconsistent history may signal assault/trafficking; suicidal intent requires direct assessment.
topics.act: Ensure immediate safety, speak privately, use trauma-informed consent and preserve evidence when indicated. For imminent self-harm risk, maintain observation and remove hazards per protocol.
topics.remember: Do not force disclosure or confront a suspected trafficker in a way that increases danger. Explain confidentiality and required-reporting limits.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a private safe doorway offers consent, protection and direct suicide-risk assessment.

topics.title: Disaster preparedness
topics.recognize: Disasters disrupt normal staff, supply and communication systems; coordinated roles prevent duplication and unsafe actions.
topics.act: Follow incident command, the emergency operations plan and assigned scope; use drills, communication pathways and appropriate community/public-health resources.
topics.remember: Know where to report and whom to notify. Uncoordinated volunteering or independently changing roles can undermine safety and resource allocation.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine an incident-command map routes staff, supplies and communication to assigned roles.

topics.title: Disaster ethics
topics.recognize: Scarce resources can create conflicts between individual needs and population benefit, including difficult triage decisions.
topics.act: Use established allocation policies, objective criteria, team/ethics support and transparent documentation; provide comfort even when definitive treatment is limited.
topics.remember: Reassess decisions as resources and conditions change. Do not allocate based on social worth, personal preference or an unsupported prognosis.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a transparent resource scale uses objective policy while preserving comfort and dignity.

topics.title: Biologic agents, nerve agents and PPE
topics.recognize: Anthrax can cause severe systemic illness; smallpox causes a contagious febrile rash. Nerve agents are chemical agents causing cholinergic excess such as secretions, bronchospasm and weakness.
topics.act: Protect responders with hazard-appropriate PPE, isolate/report suspected biologic threats and give agent-specific treatment/antidotes.
topics.remember: Do not classify nerve agents as bacteria. Precautions and decontamination differ by agent; anthrax and smallpox do not share identical person-to-person transmission.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine separate biologic and chemical warning labels select PPE, isolation and agent-specific treatment.

topics.title: Natural disasters and outbreaks
topics.recognize: Natural disasters create injury, displacement, sanitation and chronic-care problems. Outbreak/epidemic means disease above expected levels; pandemic describes wider international spread.
topics.act: Support surveillance, safe water/shelter, continuity of essential treatment and current public-health precautions.
topics.remember: Scale does not by itself describe severity. Verify changing guidance and coordinate reporting instead of relying on rumors or assumptions about transmission.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a widening map shows outbreak spread while safe water and continuity of care protect survivors.

topics.title: Vesicants
topics.recognize: Sulfur mustard can cause delayed skin blisters and eye/airway injury; lewisite can cause immediate pain and systemic toxicity.
topics.act: Protect responders, remove contaminated clothing and follow agent-specific decontamination; irrigate eyes and support airway, burns, pain and fluids as indicated.
topics.remember: Absence of immediate pain does not exclude mustard exposure. Do not confuse pulmonary phosgene with vesicant phosgene oxime.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine delayed blister stamps warn that absent immediate pain does not exclude mustard exposure.

topics.title: Decontamination
topics.recognize: Contaminants can keep injuring the patient and spread to staff/equipment; decontamination removes the agent and limits secondary exposure.
topics.act: Use hot/warm/cold zones and proper PPE; remove/bag clothing and use dry or water-based methods appropriate to the agent while protecting privacy and temperature.
topics.remember: Airway support, hemorrhage control or antidotes may occur alongside protected decontamination. Do not delay every lifesaving intervention until washing finishes.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine dirty-to-clean zones remove contaminants while protected teams continue lifesaving care.

topics.title: Four shock mechanisms
covers: Risk factors for the development of all types of shock
topics.recognize: Hypovolemic loses volume; cardiogenic loses pump function; distributive loses vascular tone; obstructive blocks blood flow. Risks include bleeding, infarction, infection/anaphylaxis and mechanical obstruction.
topics.act: Recognize poor perfusion and rapidly identify the mechanism while supporting ABCs.
topics.remember: A low blood pressure is not the only clue: altered mentation, reduced urine and abnormal perfusion can appear earlier. Different mechanisms need different fluid and definitive treatment plans.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine empty tank, broken pump, wide pipes and blocked flow represent four shock mechanisms.

topics.title: Cardiogenic shock
topics.recognize: Pump failure produces low output, often with pulmonary congestion; myocardial infarction is an important trigger.
topics.act: Support oxygenation, ECG/hemodynamic monitoring and urgent cause-directed therapy; give ordered vasoactive or mechanical support.
topics.remember: The tank may already be full. Large indiscriminate fluid boluses can worsen congestion; treatment follows volume assessment and the failing pump's cause.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a failing pump backs fluid into the lungs; adding fluid blindly can worsen congestion.

topics.title: Septic and anaphylactic shock
topics.recognize: Distributive shock involves vasodilation and maldistributed flow. Sepsis adds infection-related organ dysfunction; anaphylaxis can add airway swelling/bronchospasm.
topics.act: Sepsis: urgent assessment, prescribed cultures/antibiotics, fluids and vasopressors. Anaphylaxis: prompt IM epinephrine, emergency response and airway/circulation support.
topics.remember: Early septic shock can have warm skin. Similar hypotension does not make these conditions interchangeable; treat the underlying mechanism immediately.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine widened pipes reduce effective pressure; infection and allergy require different urgent treatments.

handout.caption: From your guides · Septic Shock: Why Organs Are At Risk

topics.title: Hypovolemic shock
topics.recognize: Blood or fluid loss lowers preload and output, causing tachycardia, cool skin, reduced urine and worsening mental status.
topics.act: Control the source of loss and administer prescribed volume replacement; use blood products for significant hemorrhage as indicated.
topics.remember: Trend perfusion rather than relying on one BP. Replacing volume without stopping ongoing bleeding or fluid loss does not resolve the cause.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a leaking tank needs the leak stopped and prescribed volume replaced.

topics.title: Obstructive shock
topics.recognize: Mechanical blockage prevents filling or forward flow; examples include pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax.
topics.act: Support ABCs and arrange urgent cause-specific relief through the emergency team.
topics.remember: The pump may be intrinsically functional but cannot move blood past the obstruction. Fluids or pressors alone cannot definitively fix every mechanical cause.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a blocked pipe prevents forward flow until its mechanical obstruction is relieved.

handout.caption: From your guides · Tension pneumothorax

topics.title: Stages and progression of shock
covers: Manifestations of shock in each stage
topics.recognize: Inadequate cellular oxygen delivery leads to anaerobic metabolism and organ dysfunction. Compensation can preserve BP initially; progressive shock causes hypotension, oliguria and worsening mental status; refractory shock has severe irreversible injury.
topics.act: Track perfusion, lactate trends, urine output and response while treating the cause.
topics.remember: Do not wait for hypotension to recognize shock. Stages describe a continuum rather than a reason to postpone intervention.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine perfusion warning lights worsen before the pressure gauge finally falls.

topics.title: Shock diagnostics and treatment
covers: Nursing management of and priorities of care for clients with all types of shock (general and specific)
Inotropic & vasoactive agents used in the treatment of shock
topics.recognize: Examination, ECG, lactate, blood gas, CBC/chemistry, cultures or imaging help identify impaired perfusion and its cause.
topics.act: Monitor response to prescribed fluids, oxygen/ventilation and cause-directed treatment; titrate vasoactive/inotropic therapy to ordered targets with close perfusion and access-site checks.
topics.remember: Vasopressors raise vascular tone; inotropes improve contractility. Drug and fluid choices depend on mechanism, volume status and response, not one universal shock recipe.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine a pump-strength lever and vessel-tone lever represent different vasoactive treatment effects.

topics.title: MODS
covers: Risk factors for the development of MODS
topics.recognize: Persistent inflammatory/perfusion injury after sepsis, trauma or other severe illness can cause progressive dysfunction of two or more organ systems.
topics.act: Treat the initiating cause and provide organ support; monitor respiratory, renal, cardiovascular, hepatic, coagulation and neurologic trends.
topics.remember: A single normal measurement does not exclude an evolving multisystem pattern. Prevent secondary injury, reassess treatment response and coordinate multidisciplinary care.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine several organ gauges fail together after a severe systemic insult.

handout.caption: From your guides · Primary vs secondary MODS

topics.title: MODS nursing priorities and family
covers: Nursing management of and priorities of care for clients with MODS
topics.recognize: Critical illness creates changing organ-support needs, delirium/immobility risks and major family distress.
topics.act: Trend organ function, prevent device/skin/immobility complications, support nutrition and communicate goals and prognosis with the team and family.
topics.remember: Include comfort, consent, decision-making support and patient preferences alongside technical monitoring. Evaluate whether interventions improve perfusion, function or comfort rather than merely completing tasks.
topics.mnemonic: Imagine organ monitors stand beside family chairs: support goals, comfort and communication together.
